promptHead: Athlete goal: marathon (Wexley Lakes Marathon) on Sun Nov 1 2026, 6 weeks out, target under 3:45.

new.headline: You jumped from 29 to 53 miles in one week, which is too big a leap even if it felt fine. Next week we hold volume near 42 miles, introduce marathon pace, and let the big long run settle in.

flags.title: Plan overrun
flags.detail: every run went long, totalling 53 mi against 38 mi planned, and the long run hit 20 mi instead of 15.

flags.title: Long run too hot
flags.detail: 88 percent of Sunday sat in zone 3 with heart rate drifting from 146 to 153, not the easy effort we asked for.

flags.title: Load spike
flags.detail: relative effort 423 is almost double the three-week average of 223, which is the red zone for injury risk.

flags.title: Easy share low
flags.detail: only 54 percent of time was in zones 1 and 2, well under the 80 percent we want in build.

flags.title: Calves tight Sunday night
flags.detail: no pain yet, but worth noting after the biggest week you have run.

answers.question: I ran way more than the plan and felt fine. Can I keep this up?
answers.answer: Short answer: no, not at this rate of jump. Your legs felt good because you are fitter, and that is great, but one week does not prove the body has absorbed the load; tendons, bones and the immune system lag behind how the run feels by one to three weeks. A roughly 80 percent jump in weekly miles and a doubling of relative effort is exactly the pattern that shows up as a niggle two weeks later. The safer way to keep this momentum is to grow by about 10 percent a week, keep one quality session, and let the long run step up every other week rather than every week. We have 6 weeks until race day, so the job now is to arrive healthy, not to prove the ceiling.

new.analysis:
The headline reason to pull the reins is the size of the jump, not the quality of the running. Fitness is clearly there: the threshold reps at 7:55/mi held form, and 20 mi at 10:02 with only 7 bpm of drift is a strong signal. The risk is that load went up on every single day at once, which is how most self-coached marathoners get hurt in the last month.

With 6 weeks to Wexley Lakes, the shape of the block is: one more build step, a peak long run, a cutback, a sharpening week, then taper. That means this week we hold roughly 42 mi, keep the long run at 16 mi, and swap the all-out threshold for marathon pace work so the specific race gear starts to feel normal. Marathon pace for 3:45 is about 8:35/mi, so the Wednesday middle miles and the long run finish both aim there.

Two process notes for the week. First, please run the easy days truly easy: heart rate under 145 and pace around 9:50 is the ceiling, slower is fine. Second, if the Sunday long starts drifting into zone 3 early like last week, back the pace off by 15 to 20 seconds per mile rather than pushing through; the long run only pays off when it stays aerobic.

safetyCallouts.title: Watch the calves this week.
safetyCallouts.body: Tightness after your longest ever run is normal, but if it turns into sharp or one-sided pain, or you feel a pull while running, stop and see a physio rather than training through it.
